thesis: This episode argues that sustainable competitive advantage stems from 'coaction'—the ability to invent and align with power automatically—rather than just existing scale or distribution. It highlights that successful companies like Amazon and Visa possess unique, idiosyncratic capabilities that allow them to reinvent themselves, while failures like Blockbuster and Diners Club missed these opportunities due to boardroom blunders or a lack of universal definition. The discussion emphasizes that true moats are often rare, proprietary, and rooted in material science or network effects that are hard for competitors to replicate.

claims.claim: Amazon is a huge fan and has been able to do what they do by taking risks and having some failures.
claims.quote: I think since we're back into invention, and I am a huge fan of Amazon, the fact that they've been able to do what they do, I would argue that they couldn't have done it if they weren't willing to take the risks and have some failures.

claims.claim: The movement into Amazon Web Services is invention, not based on existing competitive advantage.
claims.quote: The movement into Amazon Web Services is invention. I loved your guy's story on how there are the four different sources of starting points for Amazon. People love to think this based on some existing competitive advantage of the business, but it's really not. It's invention.

claims.claim: Amazon has been successful in AWS but also flopped with Fire Phone and lost billions on Alexa.
claims.quote: As successful as they are in AWS, they also flopped. Fire Phone, if you still remember that. They also lost billions and billions on Alexa. There's really no track record of a business who can continuously come up with successful invention.

claims.claim: Microsoft requires a billion dollar revenue product to green light new documents, which might be too late.
claims.quote: Ben: This was Microsoft. It was like, oh, unless you're going to go create a billion dollar revenue product, I'm not green lighting your document. Hamilton: Right, and usually, if it's already a billion dollar market, it's either too late.

claims.claim: 3M is a material science company with nichey idiosyncratic aspects and able to invent stuff.
claims.quote: Ben: Is 3M a good example of this lower right, where they know how to make all kinds of interesting stuff but for completely different customer bases, completely different use cases? Hamilton: My view of 3M is that they're basically a material science company. Material science is weird.

claims.claim: 3M was able to invent stuff like post-it notes but almost missed it due to marketing trial issues.
claims.quote: If you think of post-it notes, that was a not so sticky glue, and then they didn't know what the hell to do with it. It went on for years. There is a champion in the thing that just said, no, there's something great here. They almost missed it.

claims.claim: The iPhone and iPod are straight up coaction, similar capabilities, but the iPhone competes a little bit with the desktop.
claims.quote: Ben: Where would you put the iPhone in this framework? Hamilton: The iPhone and the iPod or straight up coaction, similar capabilities. They are computers in a generic sense, but the iPhone, in a functional way, does compete a little bit with the desktop.

claims.claim: Netflix into streaming as reinvention, but it's hard to do and you're usually in a counter position.
claims.quote: Netflix into streaming as reinvention. It can happen. It's hard to do. You're usually in a counter position because you've got a whole group of people that want to do it the old way, and they have a lot of power in a company, typically, because they've got the P&L.

claims.claim: AWS is a good example of coaction, which is where all the action is.
claims.quote: David: That's AWS for sure, right? Hamilton: Exactly, AWS. Ben: Wait, so this is the lower right? Hamilton: This is the lower middle. It's a bunch of not perfectly shared skills. You know quite a bit about the stuff that you need to do to get in there, but it's a different need.

claims.claim: Corning and glass technology have proprietary capabilities that align with power automatically, but that's very rare.
claims.quote: Occasionally, there are companies that have capabilities that are so proprietary, actually, that aligns with power automatically, but that's very rare. I'd say Corning and glass technology, for example. It's such a weird material science, so they can do glass stuff that other people couldn't do.

claims.claim: Blockbuster failed to exploit its distribution network and customer relationships to launch a streaming service, resulting in a failure due to boardroom blunders.
claims.quote: It could be the case that Blockbuster failed, where they had the distribution network and the customer relationships. There was a source of power there, and they failed to exploit it in using that to launch their own streaming service, which mostly is because of boardroom blunders, but a failure nonetheless.

claims.claim: Hamilton believes that if Blockbuster had done a red envelope business a year earlier, Netflix would not have survived.
claims.quote: Hamilton: My take of Blockbuster is if they'd done a red envelope business a year earlier, Netflix wouldn't have survived.

claims.claim: Hamilton and Ben discuss Diners Club as an example of a company that missed the business definition of a universal card for everything.
claims.quote: Hamilton: Do either of you have Diners Club's cards? Ben: I do not. David: No. Hamilton: Right, so they missed it. It's a great example. They didn't understand that there was actually a platform where you want to cover as many purchase types as possible, and it shouldn't be constrained. They missed the business definition.

claims.claim: Chenyi states that Visa has a 50% margin, which he finds astonishing.
claims.quote: Chenyi: Yeah, Visa's 50% margin. It's astonishing.

claims.claim: Ben expresses surprise that Visa did not IPO until the 2000s.
claims.quote: Ben: Wow. We got to do Visa at some point. I can't believe Visa didn't IPO until the 2000s.

claims.claim: Ben identifies Bank of America as the founder of BankAmericard in 1958.
claims.quote: Ben: I think it was a B of A. Yes, founded in 1958. by Bank of America as BankAmericard.

claims.claim: Ben and David discuss Nintendo's 95% market share of people buying video game consoles in the 1980s.
claims.quote: Ben: Of course, the reason that those third-party publishers are making the games for them is because they have 95% market share of people buying video game consoles.

claims.claim: Chenyi describes Amazon's retail business as having a gigantic scale advantage in infrastructure, including warehouse and distribution centers.
claims.quote: Chenyi: I'll give you an example of intertwined real life. We all know Amazon in retail has gigantic scale advantage in the infrastructure, just all the warehouse and distribution centers are built.

claims.claim: David notes that the IPO of BankAmericard happened right in the middle of the great financial crisis in March 2008.
claims.quote: David: Yeah, it was a consortium of banks. That's right. I remember all this now. The IPO happened right in the middle of the great financial crisis. It was March 2008.

claims.claim: Uber's international expansion was irrational because the core cost was acquiring customers, not technology, making each new geography a new business.
claims.quote: Back to your example of Uber, if the core power prospect of Uber is actually scale economies which says, the technology framework of doing the matching automatically is so hard and it acquires so much cost to build, then international expansion would have been totally irrational because you're just spreading that fixed cost over more geographies, and you're getting a head start in every single pla

claims.claim: The majority of Uber's cost lies in acquiring and maintaining customers, so the route to try is network economies, which are heavily bounded geographically.
claims.quote: But the truth is, it's not. The majority of cost of that business actually lies in acquiring and maintaining their customers, which means if anything, the route you should really try to get to is network economies, if you have one. The scope of that network that defines each market is actually heavily bounded geographically.

claims.claim: Uber Eats and ride sharing may belong to the same business, but it is more plausible than different geographies.
claims.quote: Chenyi: I think the jury's still out whether ride sharing and food delivery belong to the same business. Maybe they do. Hamilton: But it's more plausible than different geographies.

claims.claim: Microsoft's network scope extends to productivity software because users have high cost affiliation and enterprise-wide adoption, creating competitive hassle for Slack.
claims.quote: Because of that, Microsoft's network scope basically extends to whatever demand my user side would have without incurring more cost on their end. They don't have to do another procurement cycle, maybe or not have to buy another hardware for it. That naturally extends to, basically, maybe all of productivity software. That's how you see Microsoft teams create at least a competitive hassle for Slack

claims.claim: Slack has a good product, but good products don't always win because incumbents like Microsoft have a network that can extend into the product Slack operates in.
claims.quote: I think we all have experienced that Slack has a really good product, but good products don't always win because when there is competitive advantage from an incumbent, in the case of Microsoft, they basically have a network that can extend into the product that Slack is operating in. They create issues competitively.

claims.claim: Nintendo had an ironclad lock on distribution networks, which is the same thread through the whole business from playing cards to video games.
claims.quote: What they had, originally, that is the same thread through the whole business, is they had an absolutely ironclad lock on their distribution networks, and then over time, through playing cards into toys, into video games, into toy retailers.

claims.claim: Sony's entry into game consoles was a different business and brutally hard, relying on capabilities and engineering when analog was king.
